## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature and SuttaCentral)
*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and SuttaCentral data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*
The *Āyācitabhattajātaka* (Ja 19) is a narrative belonging to the Jātaka collection of the Pali Canon [Fausböll 1877; Sahni 2008]. According to the narrative framework, the Buddha recounted the story while dwelling at Jetavana regarding people making vows to offer sacrifices to deities [SuttaCentral; Fausböll 1877]. In this tradition, merchants venturing on business trips would sacrifice living creatures to deities and make a vow (*āyācana*) to offer another sacrifice if they returned safely and profitably; upon their successful return, they slaughtered more animals believing their success was owed to the spirits [SuttaCentral; Fausböll 1877].
In the story of the past, the Bodhisatta was reborn as a tree spirit (*rukkhadevatā*) [Sutherland 1991; Fausböll 1877]. When worshippers prepared to make animal offerings to fulfill their vows, the spirit manifested to preach against animal sacrifice, admonishing that release from a spiritual debt is not worth the severe karmic retribution resulting from slaughtering living beings, and demonstrating that true release cannot be gained through blood sacrifice [Sutherland 1991; DeCaroli 2004; Hazra 1994; Fausböll 1877]. Hearing this instruction, the people abstained from killing living beings and fulfilled ethical conduct [Fausböll 1877].
Neither SuttaCentral nor DharmaNexus identifies any early cross-language parallels or significant internal Pali text-reuse matches for this story in Chinese, Sanskrit, or Tibetan corpora [SuttaCentral; DharmaNexus].
